PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 87 — Lesson 111: Acne, Rosacea & Hidradenitis Suppurativa

FNP-level goal: Distinguish common inflammatory facial and follicular disorders by lesion morphology and distribution, prevent scarring and medication harm, address the functional and emotional burden of visible disease, and identify when urgent assessment or dermatology collaboration is safer than serial empiric treatment.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate acne vulgaris, papulopustular rosacea, folliculitis, periorificial dermatitis, and hidradenitis suppurativa through morphology, distribution, time course, and associated findings.
  • Explain the mechanisms of comedonal acne, inflammatory acne, rosacea flushing, and follicular occlusion in hidradenitis suppurativa.
  • Build safe first-line treatment plans that incorporate pregnancy potential, medication adverse effects, antimicrobial stewardship, access, and adherence.
  • Recognize scarring acne, nodulocystic disease, ocular rosacea, severe HS infection or pain, and psychosocial distress as escalation problems.
  • Use follow-up to measure not just lesion counts, but scarring, drainage, pain, sleep, work, sexual health, mood, and treatment tolerability.

Part 1 — The First Question Is: What Is the Primary Lesion?

Before naming an acne-like eruption, identify comedones, papules, pustules, nodules, cysts, plaques, diffuse erythema, telangiectasias, drainage, tunnels, or scarring. Comedones—open or closed—strongly support acne vulgaris. Papules and pustules on central facial erythema without comedones suggest rosacea. Recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, drainage, double-ended comedones, tunnels, and scars in axillae, groin, inframammary, perineal, or buttock areas should raise hidradenitis suppurativa rather than recurrent simple boils.

Diagnostic labels matter because treatment and urgency differ. A patient with HS may experience years of painful drainage and stigma if each flare is treated only as an isolated abscess. A patient with rosacea may worsen with irritating acne products. A patient with severe inflammatory acne can develop permanent scars while waiting through repeated ineffective over-the-counter trials.

Part 2 — Acne Vulgaris: Mechanism Guides Combination Treatment

Acne develops through a combination of follicular plugging, sebum production, Cutibacterium acnes–associated inflammation, and immune response. The visible spectrum ranges from comedones to inflammatory papules and pustules to deeper nodules and cysts. Distribution often involves the face, chest, shoulders, and back. Adult-onset or treatment-resistant acne warrants review of medications, menstrual pattern, hirsutism, androgen-excess symptoms, pregnancy possibility, cosmetic products, occlusion, supplement use, and psychosocial impact.

Severity is not only the number of lesions. Deep nodules, pain, scarring, post-inflammatory pigment change, large body-surface involvement, rapid progression, and major emotional distress can make apparently modest lesion counts clinically severe. Skin of color needs deliberate attention to dyspigmentation and irritation; over-aggressive treatment can worsen pigment change and reduce adherence.

Part 3 — FNP Acne Assessment

Ask about onset, distribution, lesion types, cyclic pattern, prior therapies, family history, products, picking, friction or occlusion, menstrual and endocrine history when indicated, medication and supplement use, pregnancy potential, and mental-health impact. Examine for comedones, inflammation, nodules, scars, hyperpigmentation, hirsutism, virilization, and signs of infection. Do not perform broad endocrine testing solely because a patient has acne; target evaluation to compatible clinical features.

Document baseline photographs only with consent and secure workflow. This can be useful because acne improvement is gradual. Set realistic expectations: therapies often require weeks of consistent use before meaningful change, and early dryness or irritation may be managed by adjusting application frequency, vehicle, and barrier support rather than abandoning a helpful regimen immediately.

Part 4 — First-Line Acne Care and Medication Safety

Topical retinoids help address comedonal disease and are commonly part of maintenance plans when clinically appropriate. Benzoyl peroxide can reduce inflammatory burden and helps reduce antimicrobial resistance pressure when topical or oral antibiotics are used. Combining therapies that target different mechanisms is often more rational than using an antibiotic alone. Oral antibiotics, when selected for moderate to severe inflammatory acne, should be time-limited and combined with nonantibiotic topical therapy rather than continued indefinitely without reassessment.

Review pregnancy potential and current pregnancy before prescribing or continuing acne medications with reproductive safety concerns. Do not treat a pregnancy discussion as a formality; it changes medication selection and referral planning. Systemic isotretinoin requires highly structured specialist monitoring and pregnancy-prevention requirements and is not a casual escalation for a routine primary-care refill. Severe nodulocystic acne, scarring, or failure of appropriate first-line treatment warrants dermatology collaboration early.

Part 5 — Rosacea: Not Just Adult Acne

Rosacea commonly involves central facial flushing, persistent erythema, visible vessels, papules, pustules, burning, stinging, and sensitivity. Comedones are usually absent. Triggers can include heat, alcohol, spicy foods, sun, emotional stress, exercise, and certain products, but trigger patterns vary; patients should identify their own patterns rather than adopt restrictive universal rules. Gentle skin care, sunscreen, and avoidance of irritating products are foundational.

Ask specifically about eye symptoms: gritty sensation, eye redness, tearing, recurrent styes, light sensitivity, eye pain, or visual change. Ocular rosacea can threaten comfort and, rarely, vision. Eye pain, photophobia, reduced vision, significant corneal symptoms, or severe eyelid inflammation need prompt eye-care evaluation rather than a routine dermatology referral.

Part 6 — Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Recurrent Follicular Disease, Not Poor Hygiene

HS is a chronic inflammatory follicular disease. It is not caused by poor hygiene and should not be framed as a failure of cleanliness. Typical features are recurrent painful deep nodules, abscesses, drainage, tunnels or sinus tracts, and scarring in intertriginous areas. Disease burden includes odor, dressing costs, missed work, sleep disruption, sexual-health impact, isolation, depression, and anxiety. Ask permission before examining sensitive sites and use trauma-informed, nonjudgmental language.

The FNP assesses location, frequency, duration, drainage, tunnels, scars, fever, cellulitis, pain control, smoking, metabolic disease, menstrual association, pregnancy, and prior procedures. Obesity and smoking can be associated with HS, but advice about weight or tobacco must not substitute for analgesia, anti-inflammatory care, referral, and practical support. Repeated incision and drainage may be necessary for an acute fluctuant collection, but it does not by itself provide long-term HS control.

Part 7 — HS Disposition and Longitudinal Care

Escalate urgently for systemic illness, rapidly spreading cellulitis, severe pain with concern for deep infection, immunocompromise, perineal involvement with systemic features, or inability to manage at home. Dermatology referral is appropriate for recurrent or extensive disease, tunnels, scars, frequent flares, diagnostic uncertainty, failure of initial care, or need for systemic, biologic, procedural, or surgical planning. Coordinate wound care, pain management, mental-health support, and gynecologic or colorectal input when anatomy and disease burden warrant it.

Part 8 — Differential and Common Errors

Folliculitis tends to involve follicle-centered papules or pustules and may relate to shaving, occlusion, hot tubs, or infection. Periorificial dermatitis clusters around the mouth, nose, or eyes and can be associated with topical steroid use. Gram-negative or fungal processes may enter the differential in selected contexts. Avoid assuming all pustules are bacterial and need antibiotics. Avoid high-potency topical steroids on an undiagnosed facial eruption without a clear indication; this can worsen acneiform or periorificial disease.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Scarring Inflammatory Acne

A 19-year-old has painful jawline nodules, chest lesions, early pitted scars, and avoids school events. They have used a topical antibiotic intermittently for a year without benzoyl peroxide or follow-up. The FNP assesses pregnancy potential, reviews medication use, treats the current severity with a combination and stewardship-focused plan, addresses emotional distress, and arranges dermatology referral because scarring risk changes the urgency. The outcome measured is not merely fewer papules; it is prevention of permanent harm.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Red, Burning Face

A 44-year-old reports flushing, burning, central facial erythema, and papules but no comedones. Strong acne scrubs worsen symptoms. The FNP recognizes a rosacea pattern, asks about eye symptoms and triggers, recommends a gentle barrier-focused approach with appropriate treatment options, and avoids reflexively escalating acne medications. If photophobia or vision change emerges, eye care becomes urgent.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Recurrent Axillary Boils

A 31-year-old has monthly painful axillary and groin nodules with drainage, scars, and embarrassment. They have received multiple short antibiotic courses in urgent care. The FNP identifies a likely HS pattern, assesses for acute infection and pain, provides nonstigmatizing education, connects the patient to dermatology and supportive care, and creates follow-up that addresses dressings, work impact, mood, and long-term disease control. The lesson is that recurrent site-specific abscesses may be chronic inflammatory disease.

FNP High-Yield Framework: FACE

  1. F — Find the lesion type: comedone, papule, pustule, nodule, tunnel, scar, erythema, or vascular change.
  2. A — Ask about anatomy and associations: distribution, eyes, menstrual or endocrine symptoms, products, medications, friction, and recurrence.
  3. C — Consider context and contraindications: pregnancy potential, skin tone, adverse effects, access, and mental-health burden.
  4. E — Escalate early when needed: scarring, nodules, ocular findings, HS tunnels, severe pain, infection, or major functional impact.

Take-Home Summary

Acne, rosacea, and HS are not cosmetic afterthoughts. They can produce scarring, pain, vision risk, infection concerns, and major psychosocial harm. FNP-level care starts with morphology and distribution, uses combination treatment and antibiotic stewardship thoughtfully, checks reproductive safety and ocular symptoms, and builds a referral pathway before chronic damage accumulates.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, current prescribing information, dermatology or ophthalmology consultation, procedural training, or urgent evaluation for systemic illness, severe pain, eye symptoms, rapidly spreading infection, or acute distress.
